newsitem.title: USA: PG&E chairman favours incremental growth.
newsitem.headline: PG&E chairman favours incremental growth.

text.p: Pacific Gas & Electric Co chairman Stanley Skinner said on Monday he believed in growing the utility's business incrementally, rather than through a big acquisition.

"It is prudent to have a diversified portfolio. We want to pursue smaller opportunties, where we can establish a beachhead and then grow," Skinner said during an interview at an Edison Electric Institute conference.
He said the recent purchase of a gas pipeline in Queensland, Australia, which had led to the discovery of other Australian opportunities, was an example of such a strategy.
Skinner expressed no surprise at the current wave of mergers and acquisitions sweeping the U.S. electric utility industry.
"There will be a lot more consolidation," he said.
But he warned it could take regulators and consumers another two or three years to reach a required level of tolerance and acceptability towards the changes.
"That's a long time to tie up your best people with one thing," he noted. "Do you really want to do that? Right now I don't."
Nonetheless, the benefits of consolidation were unquestionable and government and consumers would eventually become less sceptical, Skinner predicted.
PG&E had the advantage of being cash rich, Skinner said. "We are going to have excellent cash flow for at least the next five years," he said.
Under state legislation, California's investor-owned utilities can recover the cost of stranded investments from ratepayers during a 5-year period in the run-up to open market competition.
The term "stranded" applies to investments made under the existing regulatory framework, which are not expected to be profitable under market competition.
Stranded costs for California's three investor-owned utilities are estimated at more than $28 billion.
Skinner said that PG&E will employ the cash to buy-back stock, retire debt and look at other investment opportunities that will enhance shareholder value.
He said PG&E was a supporter of deregulation, "even though earnings will be lower and more volatile."
The utility earlier this month cut its dividend by 39 percent, citing these concerns.
In the longer term, however, Skinner anticipated more business opportunities would arise from deregulation.
He said the distribution business was attractive and that the group did not "have a philosophy against divestment."
PG&E, through its partnership with Bechtel in US Generating, was still involved the construction and operation of power plants worldwide.

"The only place we are getting out of it is in California," Skinner said. "Five years from now that market will open. If somebody else can take the plants and run them more efficiently, that's a benefit to our customers."

The utility announced last week plans to sell four natural gas-fired power plants to comply with a California Public Utilities Commission order that it divest half of its fossil- fuel generating capacity.
